definition: The junction tree algorithm (also known as 'Clique Tree') is a method used in machine learning to extract marginalization in general graphs.
details: In essence, it entails performing belief propagation on a modified graph called a junction tree. The graph is called a tree because it branches into different sections of data; nodes of variables are the branches. The basic premise is to eliminate cycles by clustering them into single nodes. Multiple extensive classes of queries can be compiled at the same time into larger structures of data. There are different algorithms to meet specific needs and for what needs to be calculated. Inference algorithms gather new developments in the data and calculate it based on the new information provided.

explainer.lead: An exact inference method that makes hard probabilistic queries tractable in graphs with cycles. It matters because general graphs cannot be handled by naive belief propagation without correction.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a tangled spiderweb; you bundle the knots into a few big clumps and connect those clumps in a branching pattern, so messages can pass cleanly instead of looping forever.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers build a junction tree by clustering the cycles into single nodes and then run belief propagation over it; a common pitfall is that the clusters can grow very large, making the method expensive on densely connected graphs.
tiers.paperLevel: Definition: compile the graph into a tree of cliques (the junction tree) and perform belief propagation on it; multiple extensive classes of queries can be compiled at the same time into larger structures of data, and different algorithms exist for different computations. Known limit: it works by eliminating cycles via clustering, so cost scales with the size of the clusters.

explainer.example: For a graph whose variables form a loop, the cycle is merged into one clique node, and messages passed along the resulting tree yield the marginals.
